subject: chemistry
title: Neutralisation Reactions
welcome_lead: Mix the right acid and alkali and they cancel out, making salt and water.
meta_desc: Master neutralisation reactions in this KS3 chemistry adventure on acids and alkalis.
final_note: You can now write the general equation for any neutralisation.

concepts.def: Acid + alkali react to give salt + water.
A compound made from the metal in the alkali and the acid.
Antacid tablets neutralise excess stomach acid.

walkthroughs.body_html:
When an acid reacts with an alkali, the result is always:

acid + alkali → salt + water

The pH moves towards 7 as they neutralise each other.

The acid decides the second part of the salt's name:

HCl → chloride. H₂SO₄ → sulfate. HNO₃ → nitrate.

Example: sodium hydroxide + HCl → sodium chloride + water.
Antacids neutralise stomach acid to ease indigestion. Farmers add lime (an alkali) to soil that is too acidic. Toothpaste neutralises the acids made by bacteria on your teeth.

options: Salt + water
Just water
Just salt
A new acid

mcqs.q: How do alkenes typically react with bromine?
options: Bromine substitutes for a hydrogen on the alkene, releasing HBr.
The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
The order of reaction is always equal to the number of reactants in the equation.
By electrophilic addition — bromine adds across the double bond to form a dibromoalkane.

mcqs.q: What happens to electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine?
options: Sodium and chlorine share an electron between them.
The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Sodium loses one electron to chlorine; the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions attract electrostatically.
